claims.statement: The integration_settings table is keyed by a stable string `key` and stores `encrypted_value` plus `is_secret`, `updated_by`, and timestamps; per-Page Facebook tokens are dynamic rows keyed by `facebook_page_token:<page_id>`.

IntegrationSettingsCipher wraps every secret in AES-GCM with a 12-byte random nonce and stores the result as `v1:<base64(nonce||ciphertext)>`; the key is `SHA-256(integration_settings_encryption_key or jwt_secret)`. The cipher itself does not consult `app_env`; the production gate is in `Settings.model_post_init`, which refuses to boot production with an empty `integration_settings_encryption_key`, and refuses to boot with the dev default `jwt_secret` unless `app_env == "development"`.

Settings.model_post_init refuses to boot when `app_env != "development"` and either `jwt_secret` remains the committed dev default or `integration_settings_encryption_key` is empty, so a production instance cannot sign admin JWTs with a public key or skip encryption.

Per-Page Facebook tokens are stored as `v2:` rows whose AEAD associated data is the Page id, so a ciphertext produced for Page A fails to decrypt under Page B (`InvalidTag`). The Page-token resolution path `_stored_value_with_context` inside `IntegrationSettingsService.resolve_facebook(page_id)` rejects legacy `v1:` rows outright with a warning and returns empty; the general `decrypt_with_context` helper still falls back to the legacy `v1:` decrypt for callers that do not need AAD binding.

Per-provider admin views (`IntegrationSettingsService.admin_view`, `admin_minimax_view`, `admin_openrouter_view`, `admin_custom_llm_view`, `admin_facebook_oauth_view`) return only `{configured: bool, preview: '<first4>...<last4>'}` for each secret; short values are fully masked with `*` via the `_preview` helper. Non-secret fields (app ids, model names, base URLs, the enabled flag, the failover ranking) are surfaced verbatim. All admin endpoints are gated by `require_admin`.

Each chatbot turn builds `GraphDeps` via `graph.factories.build_deps`, which constructs an `IntegrationSettingsService` and resolves runtime configs with DB rows taking precedence over `Settings` env-var fallbacks. `ZaloRuntimeConfig` is resolved per turn (cheap Redis-cached via `cached_zalo_config`). `MinimaxRuntimeConfig`, `OpenRouterRuntimeConfig`, and `CustomLlmRuntimeConfig` are resolved inside `_build_cached_clients`, which runs only when the LLM-cache key (mm + or + fb namespace versions) flips. `FacebookRuntimeConfig` is resolved per Page by the channel-adapter layer when a conversation arrives on a multi-Page provider.

Secret-bearing caches live in `_LOCAL_SECRET_CACHE` keyed by `namespace + version + key_prefix` (LRU, capped at 16 entries per process) and never enter Redis. The LLM-client cache in `_build_cached_clients` is keyed by all three provider namespace versions — `mm:<v> | or:<v> | fb:<v>` — covering `integration_minimax`, `integration_openrouter`, and `integration_custom_llm`; Zalo is deliberately excluded so an OA token rotation does not tear down the cached LLM clients. When the key flips, displaced bundles are scheduled for retirement behind a 600s grace window so in-flight turns can finish.

ZaloChannelSender receives a `refresh=lambda: integration_settings.refresh_oa_access_token()` closure; refresh is guarded by a Redis `SET NX EX` lock so RQ workers do not refresh in parallel, and losers re-read the token the winner just stored.

Admin updates encrypt the value, upsert the IntegrationSetting row, record an audit row tagged `update_zalo_integration_settings` listing changed keys (never values), commit, evict the local cache namespace, and bump the namespace version so subsequent reads decrypt fresh.

Decrypt failures (`InvalidTag`) are caught, logged with the key name only, and the row is skipped so callers fall back to env vars instead of 500ing the admin view; key rotation therefore requires a maintenance window that re-writes affected rows.

Four providers compete for one active slot per turn: `_SELECTABLE_PROVIDERS = {minimax, openrouter, custom}` and `_CANONICAL_PROVIDER_ORDER = (minimax, openrouter, custom)`. `llm_default_provider` selects the active provider; an unrecognised stored value falls back to `minimax`. The operator-ranked failover order `llm_failover_order` (CSV) is parsed by `normalize_llm_failover_order` into a full canonical permutation — unknown or stale names are dropped, duplicates collapse to first occurrence, unranked providers trail in canonical order — so `_build_failover_chain` can rank candidates without special cases.

CustomLlmRuntimeConfig is an operator-supplied OpenAI-compatible failover provider. `usable` is `enabled and api_key and base_url and agent_model`; `safety_model` and `fast_model` mirror `agent_model` unconditionally so a stray stored/env value (e.g. a browser autofill) can never reach a request. The label defaults to *Dự phòng* so the failover board stays readable when the operator does not set one.

`record_provider_test_result` / `get_provider_test_result` persist ONE real-probe outcome per provider (`minimax_last_test`, `openrouter_last_test`, `custom_llm_last_test`) as plaintext JSON so the settings page can render "tested 2 minutes ago · 412 ms" across reloads. Both pass and fail are persisted so a dead provider keeps showing its error. The probe runs an actual chat completion via `probe_openai_compatible_chat`, replacing the old key-presence checks. The custom-llm test endpoint also accepts operator-typed credentials in the body so values can be validated BEFORE being saved.

When `llm_default_provider` is part of an admin save, every provider snapshot must be invalidated — not just the namespace the operator wrote into — otherwise the routing flip stays stale until the snapshot TTL expires, exactly during the quota emergency the flip is for. `_bump_provider_namespaces(primary, changed)` enforces this: if `LLM_DEFAULT_PROVIDER` is in `changed`, every cached snapshot (`integration_minimax`, `integration_openrouter`, `integration_custom_llm`) is evicted and bumped; otherwise only the primary namespace is touched.

Saving `zalo_bot_token` or `zalo_bot_webhook_secret` calls `_sync_bot_webhook(settings_service, changed)`, which pushes the just-saved webhook secret to Zalo via `setWebhook`. Saving alone updates only the app side; a mismatch silently 401-drops every inbound. The re-sync only fires when the bot token or webhook secret was just changed, and it is best-effort: a failure is surfaced as a status flag on the response and never raises because the DB save has already committed.

Zalo OA refresh uses a dedicated `zalo_oa_token` HTTP client, kept separate from the runtime OA sender because the token endpoint lives on a different host (`oauth.zaloapp.com` vs `openapi.zalo.me`) and uses a different auth shape (`secret_key` header, not `access_token`). Persistence order is intentional: the rotated pair is committed BEFORE audit and cache-version bump, so losing the new single-use refresh token to an audit failure would force manual re-authorization.

Facebook Page access tokens are written via `stage_facebook_page_token_upsert(page_id, token, updated_by)`, which writes the pre-sealed `v2:` ciphertext directly (NOT via `_write_setting`, which would double-encrypt) inside a `pg.insert(...).on_conflict_do_update` statement. The caller owns commit/rollback so this can compose with other writes inside a single transaction. After commit, `set_facebook_page_token` calls `invalidate_facebook_cache` to evict the local Facebook namespace and bump the version; the lifecycle flow commits the DB transaction first and treats the Redis version bump as best-effort so a cache failure cannot roll back a successful write.
